ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Overall, 229 studies with 2,294 effect sizes from 230,492 participants were included in the present meta-analysis (see Table 2 for details).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Overall, 229 studies with 2,294 effect sizes from 230,492 participants were included in the present meta-analysis (see Table 2 for details).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports
Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

The code files load 10 distinct packages/libraries: combinat, dplyr, metafor, metaforest, psych, questionr, RcppAlgos, readxl, tidyverse, writexl. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an `renv.lock` (via the `renv` package), a `sessionInfo()` text dump, or a `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin alongside the code.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 77 columns across 3 data files.
#### Issues Identified
3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("data_all.xlsx", "data_all.xlsx", "spline_approach_all.RData" ), Column = c("DataName", "Trait", "mods"), Issues = c("🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: Adhoc/adhoc", "🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: extraversion/Extraversion", "↔️ Whitespace — 15 values with leading/trailing whitespace: \"~ T2_lag" )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 7 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}

), "Runs after" = c("—", "01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", 
"01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R", "01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R",

"—"), Basis = c("numeric", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", 
"dependency", "dependency", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Missing inputs
1 input file the code reads is in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.

```{r}

table <- structure(list(File = "data_new.xlsx", Status = "absent", Reason = "referenced file is not present in the repository, but a similarly-named file exists: data_all.xlsx"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------

```
#### Files the deposit does not hold

The scripts that did not run through read 2 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `2024-02-23 codingsheet bleidorn_lukas.xlsx`, `2024-02-23 codingsheet roberts_lukas.xlsx`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 7 scripts: 0 ran without error, 7 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 

*a script hit a `could not find function "..."` error; we added the `library()` calls it needs (see below), and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

```{r}
), Outcome = c("errored", "errored", "errored", "errored", "errored",

"runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "undefined_variable"), "Time (s)" = c(3.4, 
3, 2.9, 3, 2.8, 3, 3.5)), row.names = c(NA, -7L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Supplement_IndDiff.R", "Missing variable" = "kable_styling", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**6 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("06 SplineApproach_Open.R", "04 SplineApproach_Extra.R", 
"05 SplineApproach_Neuro.R", "02 SplineApproach_Agree.R", "03 SplineApproach_Consc.R", 
"01 Data Preparation_MetaAnalysis.R"), "setwd() removed" = c(2L, 
2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 3L), "Path(s) it set" = c("(non-literal)", "(non-literal)", 
"(non-literal)", "(non-literal)", "(non-literal)", "(non-literal)"
)), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`library()` calls added**

**1 script uses functions from packages it does not load itself.** The packages are usually loaded in another script of the project, which only helps when the scripts run in one R session in the right order. To run it we added the `library()` calls below at the top. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after adding `library()` calls it should make itself**.

text.text: for sharing their existing meta-analytic datasets on personality development.
Furthermore, we would like to thank Marco J. Altorfer for his help with preparing the meta-analytic dataset for subjective well-being.
This meta-analysis shows that, at each age, people differ from each other in how their personality traits change, with the most pronounced differences among people found in childhood and adolescence.

Teachers, educators, and practitioners should thus be aware that typical personality trait changes do not apply to every individual, illustrating a need to better understand why people differ in their personality trajectories across the lifespan.

Personality traitspatterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviorswere once conceptualized as stable constructs that do not or only rarely change in adulthood (Allport, 1961; James, 1890; McCrae et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Personality traitspatterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviorswere once conceptualized as stable constructs that do not or only rarely change in adulthood <ref type="bibr">(Allport, 1961;</ref> <ref type="bibr">James, 1890;</ref> <ref type="bibr">McCrae et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: However, this conception of traits as stable entities has been challenged by comprehensive longitudinal meta-analyses showing that personality traits change across the lifespan.

Specifically, both the rank-orders and the mean-levels of personality traits follow predictable patterns across time lags between assessments and age (Anusic & Schimmack, 2016; Bleidorn et al., 2022; Roberts et al., 2006; Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000).
text.formatted: Specifically, both the rank-orders and the mean-levels of personality traits follow predictable patterns across time lags between assessments and age <ref type="bibr">(Anusic & Schimmack, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Roberts et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: These meta-analytic findings provide a solid, yet incomplete description of personality development.

To more fully understand the ways personality traits develop across the lifespan, it is helpful to consider a third indicator of personality development, individual differences in personality trait changes (e.g., Bleidorn et al., 2021; Borghuis et al., 2017; Damian et al., 2019; Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024; Mroczek & Spiro, 2003).
text.formatted: To more fully understand the ways personality traits develop across the lifespan, it is helpful to consider a third indicator of personality development, individual differences in personality trait changes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bleidorn et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Borghuis et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Damian et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mroczek & Spiro, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Individual differences in personality trait changes bridge sample-level and individual-level description of personality development as they provide information about whether and how people deviate from the mean-level trajectory (Bleidorn et al., 2022; Graham et al., 2020; Roberts & Mroczek, 2008).
text.formatted: Individual differences in personality trait changes bridge sample-level and individual-level description of personality development as they provide information about whether and how people deviate from the mean-level trajectory <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Graham et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & Mroczek, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: For example, mean-level findings in both large-scale longitudinal studies and meta-analytic research suggest that neuroticism decreases on average in adolescence and young adulthood (Bleidorn et al., 2022; Roberts et al., 2006; Seifert et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, mean-level findings in both large-scale longitudinal studies and meta-analytic research suggest that neuroticism decreases on average in adolescence and young adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Roberts et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Seifert et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, whereas some people may experience particularly sharp decreases, for others, neuroticism stays relatively stable or even increase (Borghuis et al., 2017; Graham et al., 2020; Roemer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, whereas some people may experience particularly sharp decreases, for others, neuroticism stays relatively stable or even increase <ref type="bibr">(Borghuis et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Graham et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roemer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In nearly all studies of personality development, individual differences in change were statistically significant, providing a clear indication that personality development varies across people.
But to date, no meta-analytic investigation has synthesized these findings across studies to quantify the degree to which development varies across people nor the moderators of this variability.

A comprehensive understanding of the overall magnitude of individual differences in personality trait changes as well as moderators of these individual difference is crucial, because it is the foundation for research aimed at identifying the factors that may cause these deviations from the average trajectory (Bleidorn, 2024; Bleidorn et al., 2021; Damian et al., 2019).
text.formatted: A comprehensive understanding of the overall magnitude of individual differences in personality trait changes as well as moderators of these individual difference is crucial, because it is the foundation for research aimed at identifying the factors that may cause these deviations from the average trajectory <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bleidorn, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bleidorn et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Damian et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, identifying life stages with greater or lesser individual differences in personality trait changes offers important insights into the relative contribution of idiosyncratic sources of personality development across the lifespan.
Relatedly, personality development theories can be evaluated regarding their utility to explain differential personality development.

The examination of individual differences in change may also guide future research by identifying samples or study designs that may be particularly fruitful to investigate the sources and moderators of personality development.

For example, if individual differences in change are especially strong among certain samples, future investigation could target these samples to identify the sources of differential personality development.

In the present meta-analysis, we examined the magnitude of individual differences in personality trait changes in general and whether these individual differences vary as a function of age, time lag between assessments, trait, or methodological factors such as time of publication, sample, or assessment characteristics.

The questions of whether and how personality traits change has gained considerable research interest over the past decades (Allemand et al., 2007; Bleidorn, 2012; Borghuis et al., 2017; Fraley & Roberts, 2005; Seifert et al., 2024), with most research focusing on the Big Five traits: agreeableness, conscientiousness, extraversion, neuroticism/emotional stability, and openness (Bleidorn, 2024; Soto & John, 2017).
text.formatted: The questions of whether and how personality traits change has gained considerable research interest over the past decades <ref type="bibr">(Allemand et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bleidorn, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Borghuis et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fraley & Roberts, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Seifert et al., 2024)</ref>, with most research focusing on the Big Five traits: agreeableness, conscientiousness, extraversion, neuroticism/emotional stability, and openness <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bleidorn, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Soto & John, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Using the Big Five taxonomy as an organizing framework, comprehensive meta-analyses have integrated evidence from longitudinal studies to illustrate how rank-orders and mean-levels of personality traits develop from childhood to old adulthood (Anusic & Schimmack, 2016; Bleidorn et al., 2022; Roberts et al., 2006; Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000).
text.formatted: Using the Big Five taxonomy as an organizing framework, comprehensive meta-analyses have integrated evidence from longitudinal studies to illustrate how rank-orders and mean-levels of personality traits develop from childhood to old adulthood <ref type="bibr">(Anusic & Schimmack, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Roberts et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Rank-order stability describes the degree to which the relative positions on traits within a sample remain stable or change over time (e.g., Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018).
text.formatted: Rank-order stability describes the degree to which the relative positions on traits within a sample remain stable or change over time <ref type="bibr">(e.g., Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The rank-order stability of personality traits has been found to be relatively high compared to other psychological constructs (Anusic & Schimmack, 2016), with stability coefficients of r = .80 over 1 year for each Big Five trait.
text.formatted: The rank-order stability of personality traits has been found to be relatively high compared to other psychological constructs <ref type="bibr">(Anusic & Schimmack, 2016)</ref>, with stability coefficients of r = .80 over 1 year for each Big Five trait.

text.text: Furthermore, rank-order stability seems to increase from childhood to young adulthood and to remain relatively high throughout the remainder of the lifespan (Bleidorn et al., 2022; Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000).
text.formatted: Furthermore, rank-order stability seems to increase from childhood to young adulthood and to remain relatively high throughout the remainder of the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analytic evidence also showed that the rank-order stability of personality traits decreases with increasing retest intervals, but bottoms out at around r = .20 over intervals of more than 50 years.
Mean-level change refers to the strength and direction of changes in personality trait scores averaged across individuals (e.g., Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018).
text.formatted: Mean-level change refers to the strength and direction of changes in personality trait scores averaged across individuals (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast to rankorder stability, the pattern of mean-level changes has been found to differ across the Big Five traits.
Specifically, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and emotional stability tend to increase in young adulthood (Roberts et al., 2006; Roberts & Nickel, 2017; Schwaba et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Specifically, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and emotional stability tend to increase in young adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Roberts et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & Nickel, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Schwaba et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, openness to experience and extraversion tend to increase through childhood and adolescence and then decrease throughout adulthood.
Furthermore, similar to changes in rankorder stability, mean-level changes increase with longer time intervals between assessments (Bleidorn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Furthermore, similar to changes in rankorder stability, mean-level changes increase with longer time intervals between assessments <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In summary, existing meta-analyses provide a robust description of mean-level and rank-order stability of personality traits across age and time lags.

However, neither of these parameters speaks directly to the degree that individual personality trait changes deviate from population-level trends (Borghuis et al., 2017; Damian et al., 2019; Graham et al., 2020; Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018).
text.formatted: However, neither of these parameters speaks directly to the degree that individual personality trait changes deviate from population-level trends <ref type="bibr">(Borghuis et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Damian et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Graham et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Individual differences in personality trait changes quantify the degree to which individual trajectories deviate from mean-level trajectories of personality traits (Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018).
text.formatted: Individual differences in personality trait changes quantify the degree to which individual trajectories deviate from mean-level trajectories of personality traits <ref type="bibr">(Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of individual differences in personality trait changes would suggest that all people change alike and that personality development was exclusively driven by causes shared across people.

In contrast, substantial individual differences in change would suggest that people show a highly idiosyncratic personality development so that mean-level trajectories of personality traits are only weakly informative for the individual.

Furthermore, this finding would indicate that the sources of personality development act in unique ways across people and point to the importance of moderators of personality trait changes (Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Furthermore, this finding would indicate that the sources of personality development act in unique ways across people and point to the importance of moderators of personality trait changes <ref type="bibr">(Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: As such, individual differences in change provide a perspective on personality development that complements findings of rank-order and meanlevel change (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: As such, individual differences in change provide a perspective on personality development that complements findings of rank-order and meanlevel change (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: There can be individual differences in personality trait changes in the presence (top panels) or in the absence of rank-order changes (bottom panels).
Likewise, individual differences in personality trait changes can be found in the presence (right panels) or absence of mean level changes (left panels).
Different methods can be used to quantify individual differences in personality trait changes.

Individual differences in change are sometimes assessed using the reliable change index, which tallies the number of participants that changes to a substantial degree (e.g., two standard errors of measurement; Damian et al., 2019; Roemer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Individual differences in change are sometimes assessed using the reliable change index, which tallies the number of participants that changes to a substantial degree (e.g., two standard errors of measurement; <ref type="bibr">Damian et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roemer et al., 2024</ref>).

text.text: An alternative approach to quantify individual differences in change is to estimate the variability around the mean-level trajectory of personality traits, with greater variability indicating more diverse trajectories among individuals, and lesser variability indicating that individual participants tend to develop more similarly to one another.

In the present meta-analysis, we opted for this latter approach to examine individual differences in personality changes as it allows to quantify of the magnitude of individual differences in change and because it can be computed based on descriptive information provided in primary research.

Existing research consistently shows that people differ substantially in their personality trajectories (Asselmann & Specht, 2021; Denissen et al., 2019; Graham et al., 2020; Helson et al., 2002; Vaidya et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Existing research consistently shows that people differ substantially in their personality trajectories <ref type="bibr">(Asselmann & Specht, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Denissen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Graham et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Helson et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vaidya et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: However, a meta-analysis that examines the magnitude of individual differences in personality trait changes across studies with a standardized effect size metric is needed to advance our understanding of differential personality development for at least three reasons.
First, such an approach allows us to quantify the relative importance of unique versus common causes of personality development across the entire lifespan.

This approach could thus be used to evaluate and refine theoretical accounts regarding the explanation of why people do or do not differ in their personality trait changes in certain life phases (see next section for details).
Second, quantifying the degree of individual differences in personality changes with a standardized effect size provides benchmarks across studies and samples.

Such benchmarks are needed to move research beyond investigating whether a sample exhibits significant individual differences in change to more specific scientific questions about whether estimates of individual differences in change are higher or lower than typically found for certain samples or ages.

This approach can be particularly valuable for investigations of personality trajectories of specific samples like college students, job seekers, or psychotherapy patients, to advance our understanding of why certain populations may differ or converge in their personality development.
Third, a meta-analysis on individual differences in personality changes allows for examinations of sample-level and study-level moderators of individual differences in personality changes.

Information about such moderators can provide initial insights into the sources of a differential personality development and may guide design choices in future research (e.g., whether to focus on higher-or lower-order traits to examine individual differences in personality trait changes).
From a theoretical point of view, two variables should be considered as key moderators of individual differences in change across the lifespan: age and the time interval between assessments.
Note.
This figure illustrates individual differences in change in the presence and absence of mean-level changes or rank-order changes.

Existing meta-analyses on rank-order and mean-level changes of personality traits indicate that personality development depends on age (Bleidorn et al., 2022; Roberts et al., 2006; Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000).
text.formatted: Existing meta-analyses on rank-order and mean-level changes of personality traits indicate that personality development depends on age <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Roberts et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Examining whether individual differences in personality trait change also vary across age is important because it offers insights into the sources of personality development across the lifespan.

Evidence that individual differences in personality trait changes are more pronounced during a certain life phase would suggest that idiosyncratic sources of personality development are particularly important in this developmental period.

As shown by behavioral genetic studies, both genetic and reliable nonshared environmental factors (i.e., factors that make development more different, rather than more similar, across individuals) may be such idiosyncratic sources of personality development (Bleidorn et al., 2009; Briley & Tucker-Drob, 2014; Hopwood et al., 2011).
text.formatted: As shown by behavioral genetic studies, both genetic and reliable nonshared environmental factors (i.e., factors that make development more different, rather than more similar, across individuals) may be such idiosyncratic sources of personality development <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bleidorn et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Briley & Tucker-Drob, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hopwood et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: However, theoretical accounts differ in their implications of how these sources should contribute to individual differences in personality trait changes across the lifespan (see Figure 2 for an overview).
text.formatted: However, theoretical accounts differ in their implications of how these sources should contribute to individual differences in personality trait changes across the lifespan (see Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref> for an overview).

text.text: For example, the Five-Factor Theory (McCrae & Costa, 2008) proposes that personality development is caused by a genetically driven personality maturation program that should be completed around age 30, whereas environmental effects on personality development should be very rare and biologically mediated (e.g., a brain injury or a pharmacological treatment; Mõttus, 2017).
text.formatted: For example, the Five-Factor Theory <ref type="bibr">(McCrae & Costa, 2008)</ref> proposes that personality development is caused by a genetically driven personality maturation program that should be completed around age 30, whereas environmental effects on personality development should be very rare and biologically mediated (e.g., a brain injury or a pharmacological treatment; Mõttus, 2017).

text.text: Accordingly, individual differences in personality trait changes during childhood to young adulthood should be explained by genetic differences.
Thereafter, individual differences in change should largely disappear once biologically driven personality development is completed.
The Theory of Genotype → Environment Effects (Scarr & McCartney, 1983) posits that personality trait changes are primarily driven by genetically determined differences in environmental experiences.
text.formatted: The Theory of Genotype → Environment Effects <ref type="bibr">(Scarr & McCartney, 1983)</ref> posits that personality trait changes are primarily driven by genetically determined differences in environmental experiences.

text.text: Individual differences in the genetic make-up of individuals should evoke different environmental reactions throughout the lifespana constant source of individual differences in personality trait changes.
In childhood, there should be additional passive effects of genetic differences, such that parents provide a rearing environment that is correlated with the genotype of the child.
Then, during adolescence and young adulthood, individuals should become more active in selecting into environments that match their genotype.

Applying this theory to individual differences in personality change, to the degree that people select into environments that shape their predisposed personality differences, this active process may lead individuals to deviate from a normative personality trajectory and follow their own trajectory.

Thus, assuming that the active selection of environments is a particularly powerful source of differential personality trait changes, individual differences in change should be more pronounced in young adulthood than in childhood and adolescence.

Notably, according to this theoretical perspective, there should be significant individual differences in change across the entire lifespan due to other genotype-environment effects beyond active selection.

Although still acknowledging the genetic contribution to personality development, the Neo-Socioanalytic Theory (Roberts & Nickel, 2017) puts a stronger emphasizes on potential environmental influences on personality trait changes.
text.formatted: Although still acknowledging the genetic contribution to personality development, the Neo-Socioanalytic Theory (Roberts & Nickel, 2017) puts a stronger emphasizes on potential environmental influences on personality trait changes.

text.text: According to this perspective, personality traits remain malleable across the entire lifespan (Bleidorn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: According to this perspective, personality traits remain malleable across the entire lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, life events are assumed to trigger personality development by leading to changes and investments in new social roles (Bleidorn et al., 2018; Bühler et al., 2024; Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007).
text.formatted: Furthermore, life events are assumed to trigger personality development by leading to changes and investments in new social roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bleidorn et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bühler et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lodi-Smith & Roberts, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: As life events may differ in their timing, perception, sequencing, and consequences across people, the occurrence of important life events has been assumed to increase individual differences in personality changes (Bleidorn et al., 2020; Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: As life events may differ in their timing, perception, sequencing, and consequences across people, the occurrence of important life events has been assumed to increase individual differences in personality changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bleidorn et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, genetic and environmental influences may interact in shaping personality development, which may also explain why people differ in their personality development even when experiencing similar life events (Briley & Tucker-Drob, 2014; Kandler & Zapko-Willmes, 2017).
text.formatted: Moreover, genetic and environmental influences may interact in shaping personality development, which may also explain why people differ in their personality development even when experiencing similar life events <ref type="bibr">(Briley & Tucker-Drob, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kandler & Zapko-Willmes, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Perspectives that highlight the role of environmental causes thus imply individual differences in personality trait changes to be most pronounced in young adulthood and potentially also in old age, because psychologically relevant life experiences, such as graduation, marriage, retirement, or widowhood, tend to occur more frequently in these life phases than in middle adulthood (Elder, 1998; Haehner, Schaefer, et al., 2024; Hutteman et al., 2014; Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018).
text.formatted: Perspectives that highlight the role of environmental causes thus imply individual differences in personality trait changes to be most pronounced in young adulthood and potentially also in old age, because psychologically relevant life experiences, such as graduation, marriage, retirement, or widowhood, tend to occur more frequently in these life phases than in middle adulthood <ref type="bibr">(Elder, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Haehner, Schaefer, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hutteman et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Empirically, the question of whether and how individual differences in personality trait changes vary across age has received relatively little attention.

Using nationallyrepresentative data from 16 to 84 year-old Dutch participants, Schwaba and Bleidorn (2018) found that individual differences in change were most prominent in young adulthood and least prominent in old age for four of the Big Five traits; for neuroticism, individual differences in change remained stable throughout the adult life span.
text.formatted: Using nationallyrepresentative data from 16 to 84 year-old Dutch participants, Schwaba and <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bleidorn (2018)</ref> found that individual differences in change were most prominent in young adulthood and least prominent in old age for four of the Big Five traits; for neuroticism, individual differences in change remained stable throughout the adult life span.

text.text: Similarly, across five different representative panel studies, Wright and Jackson (2025) showed that individual differences in personality trait changes tend to decrease with age.
text.formatted: Similarly, across five different representative panel studies, <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Wright and Jackson (2025)</ref> showed that individual differences in personality trait changes tend to decrease with age.

text.text: Finally, in a study comparing emerging adulthood (16 to 19 years) and young adulthood (26 to 29 years), Pusch et al. (2019) reported that individual differences in personality changes were consistently high for neuroticism and agreeableness but tend to decrease with age for other traits.
text.formatted: Finally, in a study comparing emerging adulthood (16 to 19 years) and young adulthood (26 to 29 years), <ref type="bibr">Pusch et al. (2019)</ref> reported that individual differences in personality changes were consistently high for neuroticism and agreeableness but tend to decrease with age for other traits.

text.text: In summary, theories of personality development and initial empirical research suggest that individual differences in personality trait changes are more pronounced in adolescence and young adulthood compared to middle and old adulthood (McCrae & Costa, 2008; Roberts & Nickel, 2017; Scarr & McCartney, 1983; Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018).
text.formatted: In summary, theories of personality development and initial empirical research suggest that individual differences in personality trait changes are more pronounced in adolescence and young adulthood compared to middle and old adulthood <ref type="bibr">(McCrae & Costa, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & Nickel, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Scarr & McCartney, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, even though theoretical accounts converge on this general prediction, they differ in their claims regarding the precise trajectory of individual differences in personality change across the lifespan (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: However, even though theoretical accounts converge on this general prediction, they differ in their claims regarding the precise trajectory of individual differences in personality change across the lifespan (see Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Furthermore, theoretical accounts often lack explicit statements about individual differences in personality trait changes so that auxiliary assumptions are needed to derive testable hypotheses about personality development (Bleidorn, 2024).
text.formatted: Furthermore, theoretical accounts often lack explicit statements about individual differences in personality trait changes so that auxiliary assumptions are needed to derive testable hypotheses about personality development <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bleidorn, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, individual studies are limited in that they rarely sample changes across the entire lifespan, providing limited insights into individual differences in personality changes in childhood and old age.

A meta-analytic aggregation of research on individual differences in personality trait change across the lifespan is thus needed to test and refine theoretical predictions about when and for which traits differential personality development is most pronounced.
However, when integrating findings across studies, not only age but also the time lag between assessments must be considered in order to disentangle age and time-related differences.
Theoretical Perspectives on the Development of Individual Differences in Personality Changes Across the Lifespan Note.

This figure summarizes theoretical predictions about personality development and illustrates implications for the development of individual differences in personality changes (IDC) across the lifespan.
As most theoretical accounts lacked clear predictions on the development of individual differences in change, we had to make auxiliary assumptions.
For each theory, we included two different predicted trajectories based on two different sets of auxiliary assumptions.
Examining the time lag between assessments in addition to age is important to disentangle whether fluctuations in individual differences in change are due to age or time (Fraley & Roberts, 2005).
text.formatted: Examining the time lag between assessments in addition to age is important to disentangle whether fluctuations in individual differences in change are due to age or time <ref type="bibr">(Fraley & Roberts, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: For example, studies of younger adults may measure personality traits more frequently than studies with older adults, and if time lag and age are not distinguished it may appear that younger people vary less in their patterns of personality change simply because they are measured more frequently.
Considering time lag in addition to age be used to test whether individual differences in personality changes decrease, increase, or remain constant over longer time intervals between assessments.
This question is relevant to gain insights into set-point theories of personality development.
Set-point theories of personality development posit that personality trait changes are temporary (Ormel et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Set-point theories of personality development posit that personality trait changes are temporary <ref type="bibr">(Ormel et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: According to a strict set point-model, people may change in their personality traits after experiencing a life event, but these changes should only be temporary as people return to their pre-event personality trait levels (e.g., Haehner, Krämer et al., 2025; Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2019).
text.formatted: According to a strict set point-model, people may change in their personality traits after experiencing a life event, but these changes should only be temporary as people return to their pre-event personality trait levels (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Haehner, Krämer et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, individual differences in personality trait changes should emerge across any time interval as some people may currently experience temporary deviations from their set-point while others do not.

However, set-point theories would not predict individual differences in change to increase with longer assessment intervals, because temporary set-point deviations are not expected to accumulate over time.

In other words, across any given time lag, some people would be expected to temporarily deviate from their personality set-point, implying no association between time lag and individual differences in trait changes.

Similarly, there should be no association between time lag and individual differences in change if measurement error was the only cause of individual differences in personality trait changes, because error is assumed to be randomly distributed over time.
That is, to the degree that measurement error contributes to individual differences in personality trait changes, it does so equally across time intervals of, for example, 1, 10 or, 20 years.

In contrast, a positive association between assessment interval and individual differences in personality changes would indicate that these individual differences accumulate, providing substantive information about the nature of lifespan personality development (Roemer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In contrast, a positive association between assessment interval and individual differences in personality changes would indicate that these individual differences accumulate, providing substantive information about the nature of lifespan personality development <ref type="bibr">(Roemer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, this pattern would be in line with the corresponsive principle of personality development (Caspi et al., 2005; Roberts & Nickel, 2017).
text.formatted: Specifically, this pattern would be in line with the corresponsive principle of personality development <ref type="bibr">(Caspi et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & Nickel, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: According to this principle, people select into environments that match their initial trait levels, which are then reinforced by those environments.

Over time, these reinforcement processes may lead to diverging trait trajectories across individuals, resulting in a positive association between time lag and individual differences in personality change.
Existing evidence on personality trait change supports this possibility, showing that both rank-order of and mean-level changes in personality traits accumulate over time (Bleidorn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Existing evidence on personality trait change supports this possibility, showing that both rank-order of and mean-level changes in personality traits accumulate over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: To date, direct evidence for associations between the assessment interval and individual differences in personality trait changes is missing.
A meta-analytic integration of research on individual differences will enable a robust examination of this relationship, while taking into account the role of age and other relevant moderators.

In addition to age and time lag between assessments, we explored the role of other potentially relevant moderators that may shape the degree to which people differ in their personality trait trajectories.
Consistent with other meta-analyses on personality development (Bleidorn et al., 2022; Haehner, Buecker, et al., 2024), we focused on publication year, sample, and assessment characteristics.
text.formatted: Consistent with other meta-analyses on personality development <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Buecker, et al., 2024)</ref>, we focused on publication year, sample, and assessment characteristics.

text.text: Publication Year.
The methods used to assess and model personality trait change have evolved over the past decades (Bleidorn, 2024; Soto & John, 2017).
text.formatted: The methods used to assess and model personality trait change have evolved over the past decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bleidorn, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Soto & John, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: As such, more recent research may be more sensitive to individual differences in personality changes than earlier studies.
We examined three sample characteristics as moderators of individual differences in personality trait changes: gender composition, representativeness, and region.

First, existing research indicated that rank-order stabilities and mean-level changes do not differ across genders (Bleidorn et al., 2022), but the association of gender with individual differences in personality trait changes has not been comprehensively examined.
text.formatted: First, existing research indicated that rank-order stabilities and mean-level changes do not differ across genders <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>, but the association of gender with individual differences in personality trait changes has not been comprehensively examined.

text.text: Second, as representative samples may be more heterogenous than convenience or student samples, individual differences in personality trait change could be more pronounced in representative samples.

Alternatively, it may be that individual differences in change are more pronounced in convenience sample studies that were specifically designed to track the personality trajectories of participants experiencing life transitions or other developmentally relevant experiences.

Third, nearly all research on personality development has been conducted in samples from Western societies, so that relatively little is known about personality development in non-Western samples (Bleidorn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Third, nearly all research on personality development has been conducted in samples from Western societies, so that relatively little is known about personality development in non-Western samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: To better understand possible cultural differences in personality development, we explored whether the region of data collection is related to individual differences in personality trait changes, with the caveat that nearly all variation is among different Western cultures.

In line with existing meta-analyses on personality development, we examined six assessment characteristics as moderators of individual differences in personality trait changes: mode of assessment, breadth of the assessed trait, reliability, whether the assessed trait is intended to capture maladaptive features of personality, coding of trait assessment, and whether the measure explicitly or only indirectly assessed Big Five traits.
First, we explored whether the mode of assessment (self-report vs. other reports) was associated with individual differences in personality trait change.
It is possible that observers are less sensitive to subtle changes in a person's personality, so that individual differences in change may be larger in self-report studies.

Second, we investigated whether individual differences in personality trait changes differed between broad domain-level traits and narrow facet-level traits. Bleidorn et al. (2022)found that the rank-orders of personality traits are less stable for facet-level than domain-level traits.
text.formatted: Second, we investigated whether individual differences in personality trait changes differed between broad domain-level traits and narrow facet-level traits. <ref type="formula">Bleidorn et al. (2022)</ref>found that the rank-orders of personality traits are less stable for facet-level than domain-level traits.

text.text: Relatedly, individual differences in narrow trait changes may be more pronounced due to individual differences in specific environmental demands.
Third, we tested whether the reliability of a measure was related to individual differences in personality trait change.

Even if there were no true individual differences in personality changes, unreliability of personality assessment over time may create spurious individual differences in personality trait changes, as measurement error may lead to deviations from the average trajectory.
Fourth, we examined differences between measures assessing normal-range personality traits (e.g., conscientiousness) and measures assessing maladaptive traits (e.g., disinhibition).

People may be more motivated to change maladaptive traits when levels are high, and maladaptive traits seem to be more sensitive to change when facing challenging environments, so that individual differences in change may be more pronounced for maladaptive than adaptative traits (Haehner, Sleep, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: People may be more motivated to change maladaptive traits when levels are high, and maladaptive traits seem to be more sensitive to change when facing challenging environments, so that individual differences in change may be more pronounced for maladaptive than adaptative traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Haehner, Sleep, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Fifth, we tested differences in personality development between scales in which high values are socially desirable (e.g., emotional stability, agreeableness) and scales in which low values are socially desirable (e.g., neuroticism, disagreeableness).

To the degree that individual differences in change differ between those scales, response biases, such as acquiescence or socially desirable responding, may have influenced results on differential personality development.

Sixth, as most modern research on personality traits is organized around the Big Five taxonomy of personality traits, and given that the Big Five represents a comprehensive framework within which trait measures can be organized, we explored whether individual differences in personality trait changes differed between measures that were designed versus not designed to specifically assess the Big Five personality traits.
In the present meta-analysis, we examined the development of individual differences in personality trait change across time lags and age.

Importantly, we used an approach that allowed us to include both studies that directly examined individual differences in personality trait change across the lifespan as well as studies that provided the necessary descriptive statistics but did not themselves estimate individual differences in change.
We addressed four research questions for each Big Five personality trait: (1) What is the magnitude of individual differences in personality trait change?
(2) Do individual differences in personality trait changes differ across age?
(3) Do individual differences in personality trait changes differ depending on the time interval between assessments?
(4) Do individual differences in personality trait changes differ across methodological moderators such as publication year, sample, or assessment characteristics?

Consistent with theories of personality development and initial empirical evidence, we tested two confirmatory hypotheses (McCrae & Costa, 2008; Roberts & Nickel, 2017; Scarr & McCartney, 1983; Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018).
text.formatted: Consistent with theories of personality development and initial empirical evidence, we tested two confirmatory hypotheses <ref type="bibr">(McCrae & Costa, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & Nickel, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Scarr & McCartney, 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: First, we expected that individual differences in personality trait change are more pronounced in young than in middle and old adulthood (Hypothesis 1).
Second, we hypothesized that individual differences in personality trait changes are more pronounced over longer retest intervals (Hypothesis 2).

Our effect size of interest is the standard deviation of a mean-level difference between two personality trait assessments (SDMD), quantifying the magnitude of individual differences in personality changes.

As for example described by Eid et al. (2017), this standard deviation can be computed based on the standard deviation of a trait at T1 (SDT1), the standard deviation of a trait at T2 (SDT2) and the test-retest correlation (rT1T2):

text.text: If the test-retest correlation of a personality trait rT1T2 was missing for a certain sample, we used the results of the best-fitting piecewise model for rank-order stabilities of Bleidorn et al. (2022) to impute this correlation (Table 5 of Bleidorn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: If the test-retest correlation of a personality trait rT1T2 was missing for a certain sample, we used the results of the best-fitting piecewise model for rank-order stabilities of <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bleidorn et al. (2022)</ref> to impute this correlation (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref> of <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: That is, we estimated missing test-retest correlation based on the mean age of the sample and the time lag between assessments.

However, the standard deviation SDMD depends on the response scale of the personality trait measure: Measuring personality traits on a scale from 0 to 100 results in a larger SDMD than measuring personality traits on a scale from 1 to 5.
Therefore, we used the POMP-score transformation (Percent-Of-Maximum-Possible score; Cohen et al., 1999; Johnson & Eagly, 2014) to ensure comparability of SDMD across different response scales:
text.formatted: Therefore, we used the POMP-score transformation (Percent-Of-Maximum-Possible score; <ref type="bibr">Cohen et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Johnson & Eagly, 2014)</ref> to ensure comparability of SDMD across different response scales:

text.text: This SDPOMP score quantifies individual differences in personality trait changes relative to the maximum possible score of a scale, with higher numbers indicating more pronounced individual differences in change.
Finally, we used the escalc-function from the metafor package to log-transform the SDPOMP variable and to compute the sampling variability based on the sample size.
Using the log-transformation ensures that the sampling distribution of this effect size measure is closer to normality.
However, for interpretation purposes, we back-transformed the meta-analytic estimates.
We estimated random-effects meta-analyses with effect sizes being weighted based on the inverse of the sampling variance so that more precise effect sizes received more weight in the analyses.

As several studies contributed more than one effect size estimate, we used the three-step procedure recommended by Viechtbauer (2010) and Pustejovsky and Tipton (2022) to deal with the dependency of effect sizes.
text.formatted: As several studies contributed more than one effect size estimate, we used the three-step procedure recommended by <ref type="bibr">Viechtbauer (2010)</ref> and <ref type="bibr">Pustejovsky and Tipton (2022)</ref> to deal with the dependency of effect sizes.

text.text: First, to estimate the relationship between dependent effect sizes, we estimated the approximate variance-covariance matrix of (2) dependent effect sizes based on working assumptions on their dependencies.

As done by Haehner, Buecker, et al. (2024), we assumed that trait assessments with different retest intervals belonging to the same sample have an auto-correlation of  = .61 (Bleidorn et al., 2022) and that different traits belonging to the same Big Five domain are correlated with 1 = .48 (Pace & Brannick, 2010).
text.formatted: As done by <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Buecker, et al. (2024)</ref>, we assumed that trait assessments with different retest intervals belonging to the same sample have an auto-correlation of  = .61 <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref> and that different traits belonging to the same Big Five domain are correlated with 1 = .48 <ref type="bibr">(Pace & Brannick, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, we assumed that different assessment modes of the same trait have a correlation of 2 = .55 within the same sample (Connolly et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Finally, we assumed that different assessment modes of the same trait have a correlation of 2 = .55 within the same sample <ref type="bibr">(Connolly et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, while accurate working assumptions increase the efficacy of the meta-analytic estimations, the meta-analytic estimates remain unbiased even if these working assumptions are incorrect (Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2022).
text.formatted: Importantly, while accurate working assumptions increase the efficacy of the meta-analytic estimations, the meta-analytic estimates remain unbiased even if these working assumptions are incorrect <ref type="bibr">(Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Second, based on the approximate variancecovariance matrix of Step 1, we then estimated a multilevel meta-analytic model with effect sizes nested in studies.
Third, using the R package clubSandwich (Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2018), we estimated cluster-robust standard errors of the meta-analytic estimates.
text.formatted: Third, using the R package clubSandwich (Pustejovsky & Tipton, 2018), we estimated cluster-robust standard errors of the meta-analytic estimates.

text.text: To address Research Question 1, we estimated a meta-analytic model without any moderators to receive an overall estimate of the magnitude of individual differences in personality traits.

We had preregistered to conduct all analyses in a trait-specific way (i.e., one model for each Big Five trait) to ease interpretability compared to a model that includes trait category as a moderator.

However, to also explore whether individual differences in personality changes differed significantly across traits, we included trait category as a moderator to the meta-analytic model in an exploratory analysis.

As a second step, we examined the relevance of our key moderators age and time lag between assessments in a meta-regression framework (Research Questions 2 and 3), which we included simultaneously in the meta-analytic models.

For time lag, we subtracted 1 from the original time lag so that the intercept of the meta-analytic models describes the magnitude of individual differences in personality changes over a time interval of one year (Haehner, Buecker, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For time lag, we subtracted 1 from the original time lag so that the intercept of the meta-analytic models describes the magnitude of individual differences in personality changes over a time interval of one year <ref type="bibr">(Haehner, Buecker, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This transformation thus ensures that our meta-analytic estimates are comparable to other meta-analyses on lifespan development that estimate yearly change rates (e.g., Buecker et al., 2023; Orth et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This transformation thus ensures that our meta-analytic estimates are comparable to other meta-analyses on lifespan development that estimate yearly change rates (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Buecker et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Orth et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For age, we used a piecewise approach to examine different functional forms of the relationship between age and individual differences in personality changes (see Bleidorn et al., 2022 and Briley & Tucker-Drob, 2014 for similar procedures).
text.formatted: For age, we used a piecewise approach to examine different functional forms of the relationship between age and individual differences in personality changes (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bleidorn et al., 2022 and</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Briley &</ref> <ref type="bibr">Tucker-Drob, 2014</ref> for similar procedures).

text.text: To do so, we divided the linear age variable into different age bins.
For the most fine-grained partitioning, we divided age into 5-year bins (e.g., 1-5, 6-10) including a catchall bin for people over 75 years.

For example, a sample with a mean age of 33 years received a value of 5 for the first six age bins, a value of 3 for the seventh age bin describing ages 31 to 35 years, and a value of 0 for all other age bins.
This procedure allows different age bins to differ in their trajectory of individual differences in personality changes.
However, as a model with 16 age bins is relatively complex, we then examined whether merging certain age bins reduces model fit.
For example, we compared the fit of a meta-analytic model with one larger age bin for ages 1 to 15 years with a model with three different age bins for this age range (1-5, 6-10, 11-15).

In total, we estimated and compared all possible combinations of separating and merging the five-year age bins between the most complex model (16 five-year age bins) and the simplest model (one large age bin, corresponding to the linear age variable), resulting in a total of 32,768 models for each trait.
To compare model fit and to identify the best fitting model, we inspected AIC and BIC.

Specifically, for each personality trait, we compared the 10 models with the lowest AIC and BIC to examine whether age shows similar relations to individual differences in personality changes across traits (Haehner, Buecker, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Specifically, for each personality trait, we compared the 10 models with the lowest AIC and BIC to examine whether age shows similar relations to individual differences in personality changes across traits <ref type="bibr">(Haehner, Buecker, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In each meta-analytic model, we examined the average effect size (i.e., the intercept), the effects of moderators (i.e., the regression coefficients), and the heterogeneity of effect sizes (i.e., random effects).
The multilevel meta-analytic procedure allowed us to estimate the heterogeneity of effect sizes both within studies (𝜎 1 2 ) and between studies (𝜎 2 2 ).
We used these heterogeneity estimates to calculate pseudo-R² measures at different levels to evaluate the relevance of our moderators:

Specifically, we estimated whether a moderator reduced the amount of heterogeneity by comparing the random effect variances of a model without any moderators (Baseline-Model) and a model including the respective moderator (Moderator-Model).
In case of negative pseudo-R² estimates, we truncated these values to zero (Cheung, 2015; Viechtbauer, 2010).
text.formatted: In case of negative pseudo-R² estimates, we truncated these values to zero <ref type="bibr">(Cheung, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Viechtbauer, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As a third step, we examined the relationship between individual differences in personality changes and methodological moderators such as publication year, sample, and assessment characteristics (Research Question 4).
We incorporated these other moderators into the model with the best-fitting combination of age bins identified in the previous step.
We tested the methodological moderators one by one but also estimated an overall model including all moderators.
Table 1 provides an overview of the moderators that were examined in the present meta-analysis.

text.text: As a fourth step, we used two strategies to get insights into whether findings were potentially biased by the publication of effect sizes stemming from small samples.
First, we examined funnel plots illustrating the relationship between effect size estimates and their precision.
Without severe small-sample bias, effect sizes should be symmetrically distributed around the population effect size.
Second, we computed the Funnel Plot Asymmetry Test by including the standard error of effect sizes as predictor in the meta-regression models.

text.text: Overall, 229 studies with 2,294 effect sizes from 230,492 participants were included in the present meta-analysis (see Table 2 for details).
text.formatted: Overall, 229 studies with 2,294 effect sizes from 230,492 participants were included in the present meta-analysis (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> for details).

text.text: These studies were published between 1980 and 2023.
The samples included slightly more female participants (M = 53%, SD = 24.73%), were relatively young (M = 23.56 years, SD = 19.89) and were mostly not nationally-representative (74%).

Samples were mostly recruited in North America (39%, e.g., k = 85 in United States, k = 14 in Canada), Northern Europe (38% e.g., k = 44 in Netherlands, k = 18 in Germany), Asia (10%, e.g., k = 23 in China), and Southern Europe (9%, e.g., k = 8 in Spain).
Only a minority of studies were conducted in the Global South (4%, e.g., k = 8 in Australia).
Personality traits were mainly assessed using self-report methods (73%) with an average time lag of 2.87 years (SD = 5.09) between assessments.

text.text: As a first step, we examined the magnitude of individual differences in personality trait changes by estimating meta-analytic models without any predictors.
The results of these analyses are summarized in Table 5.
text.formatted: The results of these analyses are summarized in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref>.

text.text: Generally, the b-coefficients of our meta-analytic models are not straightforward to interpret as they were based on a log-transformation of the effect sizes.
The SDPOMP scores were back-transformed, with higher values indicating more pronounced individual differences in personality changes.
All traits had an SDPOMP score that was significantly different from zero, suggesting that there are individual differences in changes in all Big Five traits.

Furthermore, the SDPOMP scores were between 0.13 and 0.15 for all traits, indicating that, on average, people's trait trajectories deviated by 13% to 15% of the maximum score from the overall mean-level trajectory of a trait.

If, for example, a personality trait was assessed on a scale from 0 to 4, an SDPOMP score of 0.15 suggests that the mean-level change of an average person differs by 0.60 units from the overall mean-level trajectory (i.e., 0.15 x4 = 0.60).
Figure 4 provides an illustration of how SDPOMP scores of different magnitudes look like.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref> provides an illustration of how SDPOMP scores of different magnitudes look like.

text.text: Although the SDPOMP scores of the different Big Five traits were descriptively similar, we explored whether there were significant trait differences.

As illustrated in Figure 5, we found that individual differences in trait changes were significantly lower in agreeableness and openness compared to the other traits, whereas individual differences in change were significantly higher for neuroticism (see Section 3 of the https://osf.io/7wk9y/files/3sw2c for more details).

text.text: One goal of this work was to provide benchmarks that can be used to compare the extent of individual differences in personality trait changes across studies and samples.

To reach this goal, we developed a ShinyApp (https://personalityresearch.shinyapps.io/Shiny/) that allows researchers to calculate individual differences in personality trait changes in their sample consistent with the methodological approach of this meta-analysis (based on Equations 1 and 2).

To examine how individual differences in personality trait changes wax and wane across the lifespan, we included the time interval between personality assessments and the mean age of samples as moderators in our meta-analytic models.

As described above, we examined more than 30,000 possible ways of summarizing and separating age bins to identify the functional form of the relationship between age and individual differences in personality changes.

We selected the best-fitting models of this piecewise approach based on AIC and BIC and compared the findings of models with similar model fit but different sets of age bins (see Section 4 of the https://osf.io/7wk9y/files/3sw2c).
text.formatted: We selected the best-fitting models of this piecewise approach based on AIC and BIC and compared the findings of models with similar model fit but different sets of age bins (see Section 4 of the <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/7wk9y/files/3sw2c">supplementary material</ref>).

text.text: As can be seen in Table 6 and Figure 6, age showed a similar relationship to individual differences in personality changes across all Big Five traits.
text.formatted: As can be seen in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_5">6</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">6</ref>, age showed a similar relationship to individual differences in personality changes across all Big Five traits.

text.text: For agreeableness and openness, a model with two age-related variables (Age 1 to 30 and Age 30+) fitted the data best.

Individual differences in personality trait changes significantly decreased for both traits until age 30 (agreeableness: b = -0.023, p < .001; openness: b = -0.015, p = .014) and then remained flat throughout the remainder of the lifespan (agreeableness: b = 0.001, p = .827; openness: b = 0.001, p = .740).
text.formatted: Individual differences in personality trait changes significantly decreased for both traits until age 30 (agreeableness: b = -0.023, p < .001; openness: b = -0.015, p = .014) and then remained flat throughout the remainder of the lifespan (agreeableness: b = 0.001, p = .827; openness: b = 0.001, p = .740).

text.text: Similarly, for extraversion and conscientiousness, a model with two age-related variables fitted the data best but with slightly different inflection points.

For conscientiousness, individual differences in personality trait changes decreased until age 40 (b = -0.013, p = .001) and then remained flat until old age (b = -0.001, p = .826), while for extraversion individual differences in change decreased until age 55 (b = -0.008, p < .001) and then remained flat (b = 0.004, p = .284).

text.text: Finally, for neuroticism, we found that individual differences in change decreased until age 25 (b = -0.016, p < .001), continued to decrease, but less rapidly, between ages 25 and 75 (b = -0.004, p = .044), and were flat after age 75 (b = 0.017, p = .180).
text.formatted: Finally, for neuroticism, we found that individual differences in change decreased until age 25 (b = -0.016, p < .001), continued to decrease, but less rapidly, between ages 25 and 75 (b = -0.004, p = .044), and were flat after age 75 (b = 0.017, p = .180).

text.text: The general pattern of decreases in the magnitude of individual differences in personality trait changes throughout childhood and young adulthood followed by stability in the magnitude of individual differences in change during old age was consistent across models with similar fit but different age bins.
Overall, these findings were in line with our Hypothesis 1 that individual differences in trait changes are more pronounced in young adulthood than in middle and old adulthood.
However, the largest individual differences in change were not observed in young adulthood but in childhood.

Regarding time lags, we found that a longer assessment interval was related to more pronounced individual differences in personality trait changes for agreeableness (b = 0.027, p = .009), extraversion (b = 0.018, p = .001), neuroticism (b = 0.017, p < .001), and openness (b = 0.012, p = .024).
text.formatted: Regarding time lags, we found that a longer assessment interval was related to more pronounced individual differences in personality trait changes for agreeableness (b = 0.027, p = .009), extraversion (b = 0.018, p = .001), neuroticism (b = 0.017, p < .001), and openness (b = 0.012, p = .024).

text.text: For conscientiousness, the relationship between time lag and individual differences in personality changes was not statistically significant (b = 0.020, p = .071).
These results were thus largely consistent with our Hypothesis 2 that individual differences in personality trait changes are more pronounced over longer assessment intervals.
Together, age and time lag explained a substantial proportion of heterogeneity, both between studies (.15 ≤ R² Level2 ≤ .26) and within studies (.04 ≤ R² Level1 ≤ .14).

As next step, we tested methodological moderators like the publication year, the region of data collection, or the assessment mode by adding them to the best-fitting piecewise model identified in the previous step.
As preregistered, we conducted these analyses separately for each of the Big Five traits.

However, because the age-related trajectories of individual differences in change were similar across Big Five traits, we additionally conducted an exploratory analysis with moderators combined across traits.
As can be seen in Table 7, the results slightly differed across traits (see Section 5 of the https://osf.io/7wk9y/files/3sw2c for graphical illustrations).
text.formatted: As can be seen in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_6">7</ref>, the results slightly differed across traits (see Section 5 of the <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/7wk9y/files/3sw2c">supplementary materials</ref> for graphical illustrations).

text.text: The most consistent effect was that individual differences in change were smaller in magnitude for traits assessing the Big Five compared to traits not designed to assess the Big Five personality traits.

This difference was found for agreeableness (b = -0.183, p = .001), conscientiousness (b = -0.164, p = .003), extraversion (b = -0.183, p = .002), and in the combined model (b = -0.138, p = .005), but not for openness (b = -0.177, p = .074) and neuroticism (b = -0.030, p = .589).

Furthermore, individual differences in changes in conscientiousness (b = 0.184, p = .001), extraversion (b = 0.212, p = .001), and openness (b = 0.400, p = .010) were more pronounced for facets than domains, although this difference was not significant in the combined model (b = 0.126, p = .052).
Moreover, in the combined model, we found that individual differences in personality changes were lower in representative samples compared to non-representative samples (b = -0.119, p = .035).
In each of the trait-specific models, these findings were similar in direction but not statistically significant possibly due to their lower power.

Finally, there were some additional trait-specific significant effects such as individual differences in conscientiousness being lower for more reliable trait assessments, but since these effects were only found for single traits, we interpret them with caution (see Table 7 for details).
