text.text: We used two strategies to examine whether our results are influenced by the publication of results stemming from studies with small samples.
First, we visually inspected funnel plots which showed that effect sizes were systematically distributed around the population effect size.
Second, we examined the association between the standard deviation of effect sizes and effect size estimates.
This test was not significant for any of the Big Five traits (see Section 6 of the https://osf.io/7wk9y/files/3sw2c for details).
text.formatted: This test was not significant for any of the Big Five traits (see Section 6 of the <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/7wk9y/files/3sw2c">supplementary material</ref> for details).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that our results were not systematically biased by small-study effects.

Notably, heterogeneity of effect sizes across studies (e.g., as reflected by dispersion of effect sizes in the funnel plots) complicated drawing definite conclusions and other forms of publication bias could still be present in the data.

However, given that most studies included in this metaanalysis were not designed to examine individual differences in personality trait changes, it seems unlikely that the present findings effects are affected by publication bias.

Existing meta-analyses on personality development have provided convincing evidence that the rank-orders and mean-levels of personality traits change across the entire lifespan (Anusic & Schimmack, 2016; Bleidorn et al., 2022; Roberts et al., 2006; Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000).
text.formatted: Existing meta-analyses on personality development have provided convincing evidence that the rank-orders and mean-levels of personality traits change across the entire lifespan <ref type="bibr">(Anusic & Schimmack, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Roberts et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & DelVecchio, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: However, a thorough examination of individuals differences in personality trait changes across the lifespan is required to better understand the causes and course of personality development.
In the present meta-analysis, we used data from 229 studies and over 200,000 participants to examine how individual differences in personality trait changes develop across the lifespan.

We found that there are significant individual differences in change in all Big Five traits, with people differing the most in their neuroticism trajectories, and least in their agreeableness and openness trajectories.

Furthermore, for all traits, individual differences in change were most pronounced in childhood, decreased during young and middle adulthood, and then remained flat throughout the remainder of the lifespan.
Finally, individual differences in personality trait changes were stronger over longer retest intervals, for facet-level traits, and for measures not designed to specifically assess Big Five traits.

Existing research has consistently shown that people differ significantly in their personality development across the lifespan (Damian et al., 2019; Denissen et al., 2019; Roemer et al., 2024; Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018; Wright & Jackson, 2025).
text.formatted: Existing research has consistently shown that people differ significantly in their personality development across the lifespan <ref type="bibr">(Damian et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Denissen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roemer et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Wright & Jackson, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present metaanalysis confirmed this finding and extended it in two ways.

First, all Big Five domains showed significant individual differences in change (SDPOMP = 0.13 to 0.15), suggesting that there are sources of personality trait changes that lead to an idiosyncratic development in all Big Five traits (Table 5).
text.formatted: First, all Big Five domains showed significant individual differences in change (SDPOMP = 0.13 to 0.15), suggesting that there are sources of personality trait changes that lead to an idiosyncratic development in all Big Five traits (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref>).

text.text: However, our exploratory analysis also revealed small but significant differences across trait domains: Neuroticism showed the most pronounced individual differences in change, whereas individual differences in change in openness and agreeableness were lower than for the other traits (see Figure 5).
text.formatted: However, our exploratory analysis also revealed small but significant differences across trait domains: Neuroticism showed the most pronounced individual differences in change, whereas individual differences in change in openness and agreeableness were lower than for the other traits (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">5</ref>).

text.text: These subtle trait differences raise the question of whether there are sources of personality development that are more potent to change specific trait domains.

For example, in the case of neuroticism, individual differences in trait changes may be more pronounced because this trait seems to be more responsive to strong environmental influences such as negative events or psychotherapy than the other Big Five traits, potentially leading to differential patterns of personality development (Bühler et al., 2024; Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024; Haehner, Sleep, Miller, et al., 2024; Roberts et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For example, in the case of neuroticism, individual differences in trait changes may be more pronounced because this trait seems to be more responsive to strong environmental influences such as negative events or psychotherapy than the other Big Five traits, potentially leading to differential patterns of personality development <ref type="bibr">(Bühler et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Haehner, Sleep, Miller, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Roberts et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, there may be fewer life events and experiences that have differential effects on openness and agreeableness.

Second, the present meta-analysis provided benchmarks for the effect sizes of individual differences in personality trait changes that can be used for comparisons across samples, study designs, or constructs.

To facilitate such comparisons, we developed an interactive https://personalityresearch.shinyapps.io/Shiny/ that can be used to calculate individual differences in personality trait changes and compare estimates with the present meta-analytic results.
text.formatted: To facilitate such comparisons, we developed an interactive <ref type="url" target="https://personalityresearch.shinyapps.io/Shiny/">ShinyApp</ref> that can be used to calculate individual differences in personality trait changes and compare estimates with the present meta-analytic results.

text.text: Such comparisons could be used to investigate whether individual differences in change are higher or lower in specific samples, which, in turn, may advance our understanding of the sources of personality development.

For example, examining individual differences in change in samples that recently experienced an important life event may help to evaluate whether life events are a source of differential personality development (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: For example, examining individual differences in change in samples that recently experienced an important life event may help to evaluate whether life events are a source of differential personality development (see Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Similar comparisons could also be useful to better understand the effects of personality trait interventions (Haehner, Wright, & Bleidorn, 2024; Hudson, 2021; Stieger et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Similar comparisons could also be useful to better understand the effects of personality trait interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Haehner, Wright, & Bleidorn, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hudson, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stieger et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For example, significant individual differences in personality change in response to interventions would highlight the need for personalized approaches that account for personal or contextual factors that moderate intervention effects (Haehner, Wright, et al., 2025; Modersitzki et al., 2025; Nahum-Shani et al., 2015).
text.formatted: For example, significant individual differences in personality change in response to interventions would highlight the need for personalized approaches that account for personal or contextual factors that moderate intervention effects <ref type="bibr">(Haehner, Wright, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Modersitzki et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nahum-Shani et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, a comparison of the magnitude of individual differences in change across related constructs offers insights into their developmental similarity and conceptual overlap (Lawson & Robins, 2021).
text.formatted: Finally, a comparison of the magnitude of individual differences in change across related constructs offers insights into their developmental similarity and conceptual overlap <ref type="bibr">(Lawson & Robins, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: For example, recent research has compared the development of personality traits and personality functioning, including individual differences in change in these constructs, to evaluate their conceptual similarity (Haehner, Sleep, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: For example, recent research has compared the development of personality traits and personality functioning, including individual differences in change in these constructs, to evaluate their conceptual similarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Haehner, Sleep, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In general, similar change patterns across different change metrics may indicate the influence of common factors that shape the development of these constructs (Weber et al., 2023; Wright et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In general, similar change patterns across different change metrics may indicate the influence of common factors that shape the development of these constructs <ref type="bibr">(Weber et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Wright et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In summary, the present meta-analysis indicates that people differ significantly in their personality development and it provides effect sizes regarding the magnitude of the differential development of the different Big Five traits that may serve as benchmarks for future research on the sources of these individual differences.

In addition to quantifying the overall magnitude of individual differences in personality trait changes, a second goal of this meta-analysis was to evaluate the development of individual differences in personality trait changes across time lag and age.

The identification of life stages during which individual differences in personality trait changes are most pronounced offers insights into the relative importance of unique versus common causes of personality development in different life phases (Bleidorn, 2024).
text.formatted: The identification of life stages during which individual differences in personality trait changes are most pronounced offers insights into the relative importance of unique versus common causes of personality development in different life phases <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bleidorn, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We expected individual differences in personality changes to be more pronounced in young adulthood than in middle and old adulthood.
Even though this pattern emerged for most traits, individual differences in personality trait changes were most pronounced in childhood and adolescence (see Figure 6).
text.formatted: Even though this pattern emerged for most traits, individual differences in personality trait changes were most pronounced in childhood and adolescence (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">6</ref>).

text.text: These findings suggest that childhood and adolescence are life phases characterized by relatively more idiosyncratic personality development, in which individuals deviate more from the average trait trajectory than during adulthood.
The development of individual differences in personality trait changes across the lifespan did not exactly fit any of the theoretically proposed trajectories (see Figure 2).
text.formatted: The development of individual differences in personality trait changes across the lifespan did not exactly fit any of the theoretically proposed trajectories (see Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: For example, a genetically driven personality development program that is completed by age 30 as suggested by the Five-Factor Theory (McCrae & Costa, 2008) is not suited to explain why individual differences in personality trait changes were significant across the entire lifespan.
text.formatted: For example, a genetically driven personality development program that is completed by age 30 as suggested by the Five-Factor Theory <ref type="bibr">(McCrae & Costa, 2008)</ref> is not suited to explain why individual differences in personality trait changes were significant across the entire lifespan.

text.text: Likewise, extant theories that focus on environmental causes of personality development offer no explanation for why individual differences in personality trait changes were most pronounced in childhood and adolescence (Bleidorn et al., 2020; Wrzus & Roberts, 2017).
text.formatted: Likewise, extant theories that focus on environmental causes of personality development offer no explanation for why individual differences in personality trait changes were most pronounced in childhood and adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bleidorn et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Wrzus & Roberts, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Theoretical accounts emphasizing the relevance of both genetic environmental causes of personality development seem to be best suited to explain the observed lifespan trajectory of individual differences in personality trait changes (Briley & Tucker-Drob, 2014; Roberts & Jackson, 2008; Roberts & Nickel, 2017).
text.formatted: Theoretical accounts emphasizing the relevance of both genetic environmental causes of personality development seem to be best suited to explain the observed lifespan trajectory of individual differences in personality trait changes <ref type="bibr">(Briley & Tucker-Drob, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & Jackson, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roberts & Nickel, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Combined with existing evidence on mean-level and rank-order changes, the present findings refine these theoretical perspectives in two ways.

Specifically, the pronounced but decreasing levels of individual differences in personality change in childhood that coincide with increases in rank-order stability suggest that there are sources of personality development, including genetic differences, that unfold in different ways and at a different pace across children but that these sources stabilize in the first life decade (Briley & Tucker-Drob, 2014).
text.formatted: Specifically, the pronounced but decreasing levels of individual differences in personality change in childhood that coincide with increases in rank-order stability suggest that there are sources of personality development, including genetic differences, that unfold in different ways and at a different pace across children but that these sources stabilize in the first life decade <ref type="bibr">(Briley & Tucker-Drob, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, stable levels of individual differences in change from middle adulthood onward paired with mean-level increases in emotional stability and decreases in conscientiousness suggest that age-graded life experiences like parenthood in middle adulthood or cognitive decline or retirement in later adulthood may trigger directionally similar personality trait changes across people.
However, there are at least three caveats related to these interpretations.

First, auxiliary assumptions were needed to derive testable predictions about the lifespan development of individual differences in personality trait changes from existing personality development theories (Figure 2).
text.formatted: First, auxiliary assumptions were needed to derive testable predictions about the lifespan development of individual differences in personality trait changes from existing personality development theories (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: The present conclusions thus depend on the validity of these assumptions.
Second, there are systematic differences in the assessment of personality traits across the lifespan.

For example, in childhood, other-reports of temperament are frequently used to assess personality traits (e.g., Bornstein et al., 2019; Holzman, 2018; Lawson et al., 2023) whereas self-report questionnaires are more common in adulthood (e.g., Borghuis et al., 2017; Haehner, Sleep, et al., 2024; Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018).
text.formatted: For example, in childhood, other-reports of temperament are frequently used to assess personality traits (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Bornstein et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Holzman, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lawson et al., 2023)</ref> whereas self-report questionnaires are more common in adulthood (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Borghuis et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Haehner, Sleep, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These methodological differences may have contributed to the observed age-related differences in individual differences in personality trait changes.

However, they are unlikely to explain them entirely as our moderator analysis showed that assessment characteristics are only weakly related to individual differences in personality trait changes (see below for details).
Third, knowledge about the genetic and environmental contributions provide limited insights into the specific factors that drive personality development (Wagner et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Third, knowledge about the genetic and environmental contributions provide limited insights into the specific factors that drive personality development <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Wagner et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For example, within the domain of environmental factors, individual differences in personality changes could result from differences in the occurrences of important life events, differences in the ways people react to these events, and differences in how these events interact with personal dispositions (Briley & Tucker-Drob, 2014; Bühler et al., 2024; Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024; Schwaba et al., 2023).
text.formatted: For example, within the domain of environmental factors, individual differences in personality changes could result from differences in the occurrences of important life events, differences in the ways people react to these events, and differences in how these events interact with personal dispositions <ref type="bibr">(Briley & Tucker-Drob, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Bühler et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schwaba et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these considerations highlight the need for both theoretical and empirical work to better understand and explain personality trait changes across the lifespan.
The present meta-analysis may guide these efforts in three ways.

First, our study illustrates that existing verbal theories of personality development lack the precision to derive testable hypotheses about the causes and course of personality trait changes (Bleidorn, 2024).
text.formatted: First, our study illustrates that existing verbal theories of personality development lack the precision to derive testable hypotheses about the causes and course of personality trait changes <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bleidorn, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Formalized theoretical models on personality development that use mathematical expressions to describe predictors, mechanisms, and outcomes of personality trait changes would help to overcome this limitation (Eronen & Romeijn, 2020; Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019).
text.formatted: Formalized theoretical models on personality development that use mathematical expressions to describe predictors, mechanisms, and outcomes of personality trait changes would help to overcome this limitation <ref type="bibr">(Eronen & Romeijn, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Oberauer & Lewandowsky, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, such models require a broad set of robust empirical phenomena constraining the theoretical space by limiting the degrees of freedom in setting up these models (Eronen & Bringmann, 2021).
text.formatted: However, such models require a broad set of robust empirical phenomena constraining the theoretical space by limiting the degrees of freedom in setting up these models <ref type="bibr">(Eronen & Bringmann, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings are an important contribution to the development of a formalized personality development theory because they provide robust and novel insights into the temporal unfolding of personality trait changes across the lifespan (Bleidorn, 2024).
text.formatted: Our findings are an important contribution to the development of a formalized personality development theory because they provide robust and novel insights into the temporal unfolding of personality trait changes across the lifespan <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bleidorn, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For example, personality development theories need to explain why rank-order changes stabilize around age 25 while individual differences in change stabilize between age 30 to 55.

Second, our meta-analysis highlights assumptions that are necessary to translate personality development theories into predictions about the development of individual differences in personality trait changes.

For example, most research and theory to date has operated under the assumption that life events increase individual differences in personality trait changes (Denissen et al., 2019; Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024; Haehner, Wright, Krämer, et al., 2024; Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018; Van Scheppingen & Leopold, 2020).
text.formatted: For example, most research and theory to date has operated under the assumption that life events increase individual differences in personality trait changes <ref type="bibr">(Denissen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Bleidorn, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Haehner, Wright, Krämer, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schwaba & Bleidorn, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Van Scheppingen & Leopold, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, there is also some contrary evidence that individual differences in change are constant in magnitude before and after events (Jackson & Beck, 2021).
text.formatted: However, there is also some contrary evidence that individual differences in change are constant in magnitude before and after events <ref type="bibr">(Jackson & Beck, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Future research is needed to clarify these conflicting findings.
The results of this meta-analysis may facilitate such research by providing benchmarks for comparisons and insights about how study design and sample characteristics impact findings.
Third, the present results inform the design of future studies on the specific causes of personality development.

For instance, observational research on the sources of individual differences in change would be particularly fruitful in childhood and adolescence, given the larger magnitude of individual differences in personality trait changes in these as compared to later life stages.
Relatedly, research investigating trait differences may ideally focus on early middle adulthood (age 30 to age 45) when individual differences in change have leveled off in some but not all traits.
Such research could, for instance, help to identify life experiences that cause differential personality development in specific traits.
Beyond age, we examined the time interval between assessments as a moderator of individual differences in personality trait changes (Table 6).
text.formatted: Beyond age, we examined the time interval between assessments as a moderator of individual differences in personality trait changes (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_5">6</ref>).

text.text: In line with our hypothesis, we found that individual differences in personality changes increased over longer retest-intervals.
This finding is inconsistent with strict set-point models of personality development that postulate that personality changes are only temporary (Ormel et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This finding is inconsistent with strict set-point models of personality development that postulate that personality changes are only temporary <ref type="bibr">(Ormel et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: If personality trait changes were only temporary and evenly distributed across time and individuals, this developmental pattern would have implied a null relationship between assessment interval and individual differences in personality trait changes.

Furthermore, the positive association between time lag and individual differences in personality trait changes suggests that the observed individual differences in change are not just driven by measurement error but that differential personality development accumulates over time (Roberts & Nickel, 2017; Roemer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Furthermore, the positive association between time lag and individual differences in personality trait changes suggests that the observed individual differences in change are not just driven by measurement error but that differential personality development accumulates over time <ref type="bibr">(Roberts & Nickel, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Roemer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This finding is practically relevant as it illustrates that individual differences in personality changes do not vanish over time but that they are meaningful to our understanding of personality development (Bleidorn, 2024; Bleidorn et al., 2021; Schwaba et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This finding is practically relevant as it illustrates that individual differences in personality changes do not vanish over time but that they are meaningful to our understanding of personality development <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bleidorn, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bleidorn et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schwaba et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, the time interval between assessments should thus be considered when comparing the magnitude of individual differences across studiesif a study does not find significant individual differences in change, a lack of statistical power or a short timeframe between assessments may be the culprit.
Individual differences in personality trait changes also differed depending on some assessment characteristics.

Specifically, we found that individual differences in personality trait changes tended to be stronger for narrow, facet-level traits that were not designed to examine the Big Five trait taxonomy (Table 7).
text.formatted: Specifically, we found that individual differences in personality trait changes tended to be stronger for narrow, facet-level traits that were not designed to examine the Big Five trait taxonomy (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_6">7</ref>).

text.text: These findings are in line with the metaanalytic results on rank-order and mean-level stability of personality traits, suggesting that broad Big Five domains tend to be more stable than other, narrower traits (Bleidorn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: These findings are in line with the metaanalytic results on rank-order and mean-level stability of personality traits, suggesting that broad Big Five domains tend to be more stable than other, narrower traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A possible explanation for this result could be the level of aggregation: Aggregating different facets of a trait may mask the differential development of these facets so that broad traits show less pronounced individual differences in change.

However, the effect sizes of almost all methodological moderators were smaller than the effects of age and time lag, suggesting that the consideration of age and time lag is more important to understand the development of individual differences in personality changes.
The present meta-analysis has several limitations.

First, although we were able to draw on an extensive set of studies on personality development with more than 2,000 effect sizes and 200,000 participants, we still had to exclude a relatively large share of studies from existing meta-analytic datasets on personality development.
Specifically, in older studies, the minimum and the maximum score of personality trait measures, which were required for the present meta-analysis, were rarely reported.

To mitigate this problem, we contacted 130 authors to request the missing information butagain particularly for older studiesinformation on the minimum and maximum personality score was frequently not retrievable.
Second, the results of the present meta-analysis are affected by limitations of the studies it included.

Because existing research on personality development has mostly been conducted in Europe and North America, it is an open question whether our findings generalize to personality development in all cultures (Bleidorn et al., 2022; Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Because existing research on personality development has mostly been conducted in Europe and North America, it is an open question whether our findings generalize to personality development in all cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bleidorn et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Haehner, Naudé, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We tested whether individual differences in change differed across cultural contexts, but this test was underpowered to detect differences on par with the effect sizes of our other moderator variables (see Table 7).
text.formatted: We tested whether individual differences in change differed across cultural contexts, but this test was underpowered to detect differences on par with the effect sizes of our other moderator variables (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_6">7</ref>).

text.text: Future research on personality development in non-Western countries is needed to better understand which findings on personality development are culturally universal and which are specific to Western countries (Henrich et al., 2010; Van De Vijver, 2013).
text.formatted: Future research on personality development in non-Western countries is needed to better understand which findings on personality development are culturally universal and which are specific to Western countries <ref type="bibr">(Henrich et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Van De Vijver, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Third, the majority of studies included in the present meta-analysis were not designed to examine individual differences in personality changes.

As a result, we were not able to examine some theoretically interesting moderators of personality development, such as the occurrence of life events, because they were not assessed in the studies included here.
Relatedly, given our focus on personality development in the general population, we excluded studies with clinical samples and interventions.
Future meta-analytic research may extend their focus to also examine the role of individual differences in change in these populations and under these conditions.

Relatedly, we did not rate the methodological quality of included primary studies but instead examined relevant sample and assessment characteristics (e.g., reliability of the personality trait measure) as meta-analytic moderators, as we deemed this approach more appropriate for naturalistic longitudinal studies than common methods checklist.
Fourth, our meta-analytic approach relied on effect sizes that were calculated based on the descriptive statistics of personality traits assessed at two measurement occasions.
In doing so, we were able to incorporate a large number of studies, including those that were not explicitly designed to assess personality trait change.
Another advantage of this approach is that the estimates can be easily compared with those from existing and future research.

However, a potential disadvantage of this approach is that the estimates based on two assessment waves may be less reliable than estimates of individual differences in personality change derived from growth curve models and multi-level models that rely on multiple assessment waves.
For a meta-analytic aggregation of individual differences in change estimates from those models, standardized analyses and reporting practices would be required.

Fifth, by integrating effect sizes across studies, we could only investigate the effects of moderators at an aggregate level (e.g., the association between the percentage of female participants in a sample and individual differences in personality trait changes).

Individual participant data meta-analysis could be a useful step for future research to gain more finegrained insights into the conditions under which individual differences in personality trait changes emerge.
People differ in their personality development across the lifespan.
The present metaanalysis quantified the degree of these individual differences and provides benchmarks for future research (https://personalityresearch.shinyapps.io/Shiny/).
text.formatted: The present metaanalysis quantified the degree of these individual differences and provides benchmarks for future research (<ref type="url" target="https://personalityresearch.shinyapps.io/Shiny/">https://personalityresearch.shinyapps.io/Shiny/</ref>).

text.text: Individual differences in personality trait changes were most pronounced in childhood and adolescence, decreased in young adulthood, but were nonetheless significant across the entire lifespan.

These findings indicate that idiosyncratic sources of personality development are most relevant early in life, likely reflecting a combination of genetic and environmental sources of personality development.
Furthermore, individual differences in trait changes tended to increase over longer assessment intervals, suggesting an accumulation of these differences over time.

Overall, the present meta-analysis provides an initial test of different theoretical accounts of personality development and a starting point for a more systematic investigation of internal and external sources of individual differences in personality changes and for the development of formalized theoretical models of personality development.

text.text: Merging their meta-analytic datasets-as done by Haehner, Buecker, et al. (2024)-provides comprehensive descriptive information on personality development from primary empirical research.
These meta-analytic datasets were based on systematic literature searches on PsycINFO using the same search string: (personality OR trait OR temperament) AND (test-retest OR longitudinal).

Furthermore, studies were only included in the meta-analytic datasets if they fulfilled the following inclusion criteria: (1) Empirical, quantitative design (i.e., no reviews, comments, or qualitative studies) (2) Conducted with human subjects (3) Written in English (4) Longitudinal design (i.e., two or more assessments of the same sample) (5) Retest-interval of 6 months or more (6) Assessment of personality traits 1 at two or more measurement occasions (7) Nonclinical sample and no intervention (8) Homogenous age of the sample (i.e., SD of age at baseline ≤ 3) In addition, we only included studies in the present meta-analysis that reported (a) the standard deviation of a personality trait measure at baseline (T1) and a follow-up assessment (T2), (b) the minimum and maximum of the personality trait measure, (c) the age at baseline, (d) the time lag between assessments or age at T2, and (e) the sample size at T1.

As information on minimum and maximum of personality trait measures was not included in the meta-analytic datasets of Roberts et al. (2006) and Bleidorn et al. (2022), we added this information to their meta-analytic datasets in an additional coding step if available (see next section for details).
If information on the minimum and maximum was not provided, we contacted authors to request the missing information or otherwise excluded the study.
We contacted authors of 130 studies; 51 replied but only 23 authors were able to retrieve information on the minimum and maximum of the personality trait measure.
